																excellent game.

i've been a fan of this series since the first one, and the main reason i became interested in it is because i'm a huge fatal frame fan. these games took very obvious inspirations from fatal frame, and i highly recommended the first two dreadout games to other fans of fatal frame.

however, this one goes beyond that. they really expanded the concept for this latest sequel, and put more time and effort into everything. not only is there improvement in graphics and mechanics, but there is a lot more to this game that you may not expect from a horror title. there are normal non-horror segments where you're out in the town and free to explore, sometimes doing sidequests. then when the horror starts up again, you can see some inspirations from silent hill this time as well, with the normal world transforming into an "other-world."

there's also a lot more to the combat this time around, and it really goes beyond the traditional fatal frame formula by also providing melee weapons and corporeal enemies that can be attacked physically. there are also additional ways your phone can help besides taking photos to exorcise ghosts, such as a flashlight focus that stuns and knocks back enemies.

this studio did a great job improving and expanding upon the earlier games with this sequel, which is exactly what a good developer does with a series, so i'm glad to have supported them with my purchase on the release date. i hope to play more from this series in the future.

posted: july 3, 2018
																i've now played the game enough to get a feel for it. overall it has been a positive experience. i was looking for a classic turn-based style rpg and that's exactly what i got. (to be updated upon completion but here's my impressions thus far)

battle system / mechanics:
the battle system features a turn-based element similar to ffviii or lost odyssey's timing mechanic such that you have to time a button press to do full damage for every attack. it's difficult at first but once you get 20 luck for each character and some practice it becomes a lot easier.  there are several elements of the battle system which i find refreshing in fact. the guard mechanics for each character gives a specific bonus which is veryeeee useful. unlike other rpgs, i found myself guarding strategically during difficult fights to survive. another change to a common feature is spellcasting. there is no mp, instead spells known as grimoire, have casting times and a chance to be interrupted while casting. that means no casting healing spells outside of combat so items will become your best friend.

story/world:
i won't go into too much details to avoid spoilers, plus i'm less than halfway through, but the story is par for the course. ragband group of adventurers must band together to save the world. i'm playing after the rewrite so i can't speak for the original dialogue but the current dialogue is well-written. the world building elements are also captivating. i found myself thinking about the impact of story elements on the world of legrand as a whole including topics such as oppression of the poor and genocide. some elements of the story may seem a little bit cliche like the romance elements but they still have a chance to redeem themselves. also there's a world map you can walk around on. ^-^

characters:
the main characters all have unique physical and personality traits to them. i've just received my final party member and i can tell that each one of them has motivations which influence how they act. some of the characters also have hidden pasts which could come up in the future and shake things up.

graphics:
so the graphics. having grown-up playing ps1 and ps2 rpgs, i can say that the graphics are definitely nostalgic. the 2d backgrounds are certainly detailed and i like the use of live-2d over the usual static character portraits. that being said, the animation is very janky and lifeless at times. in my head, i just imagine this game coming out 15 years ago and i'm able to get past the ps2-level graphics.

other:
difficulty: this game is quite challenging and i find myself having to grind and really practice my strategy to win. some fights would be impossible without using your arcana (limit-break) so the game expects you to save it for bosses. that said i appreciate a good challenge these days.

inventory: you can only hold a limited 350 items. while it adds an element of realism, i find myself getting over-encumbered fairly quick if i don't deposit all of my items in storage before starting a new area. personally, i could do without it for quality of life.

weapon upgrading: you cannot easily equip different weapons. instead you can only change weapons when you forge a new weapon at a town from what i've seen. this kinda sucks because some weapons give different bonuses like more hp and defense as well as magic vs physcial attack which could prove useful depending on the enemies you are facing.

thanks for reading!

introduction??coffee talk is the very first visual novel i've ever played and boy! oh boy! i am blown away. i didn't expect a straightforward "reading exercise" could manage to create such a credible setting along with charismatic characters. the simplicity of the coffee talk is elegant.


a place that is only open when the sun is sleepingcoffee talk is a game about, well, coffee and talking. this visual novel takes place in the fantasy urbs of an alternative present-day seattle. a time when the war between races is but a footnote in history. when humans, elves, orcs, and vampires learned to look past their differences and coexist but radicals and racists still draw breath.

coffee talk displays some cruelties of modern life and how people are drowned in their work. it makes use of our real-life situations like racism, shootouts, gun control, parties that goes awry for young folks, and with the most noticeable one being an epidemic to further aid the credibility of its world.

you're the owner of the said café, opening your place up only after midnight that attracts a rather eclectic bunch. you're an affable barista shtick; attentive and thoughtful listener who comforts the customers by serving them warm drinks. not having a specific background on your character immensely helped the narrative to direct its focus on the customers.

																i already heard of other coffee-brewing games before, with va-11 hall-a being one of the most popular ones. however, i never got around playing any of those games before — well until now. the title "coffee talk" already includes everything you have to know about the game: it's about coffee and maybe involves a lot of talking as well. that's quite accurate as all you do is serve coffee to your customers while listening to their stories.

coffee and talking
the player slips into the role of a barista in coffee talk who owns a café. however, it's no ordinary café as it's only open at night. the reason for that is simple: there are people who are craving coffee or just need a place to stay during unusual times. although the business is, evidently, not profitable, as there are simply not enough customers during the night, the protagonist prefers to create a comfortable place nonetheless. the special thing here is that coffee talk takes place in a fantasy world with elves, orcs, mermaids, aliens, etc.

the main character
well, coffee talk doesn't have a narrator per se, however, the main character surely does feel like a passive observer who only occasionally talks to the customers. usually, i prefer more active protagonists so the reader can see them grow and can actually get to know them as this is critical for the character development. luckily, the focus in coffee talk isn't the protagonist itself but the customers who visit the café so i found it just fitting that the main character doesn't interfere in the happenings a lot but still interacts with the people if he has to.

the reader doesn't get to know the protagonist at all, although they can freely choose a name for them. everything else, however, such as gender, appearance, etc. stays mysterious throughout the playthrough. i guess that means that it's easy for the reader to imagine being the barista themselves.

what about the other characters?
the background story of the customers is getting revealed while the player serves them coffee. i found it so interesting that there are a few side-stories going on and looked forward to each new customer. you see, the same customers are visiting the café again so their story gets continued. i enjoyed that the reader gets to know the whole cast better but that's not everything, the characters are interacting with themselves a lot too. it was heart-warming to see them giving advice to each other and i sometimes just wanted to help them.

the thing i love here is that each of them has their own struggles that can be applied to the real-life as well. although the theme varies from social problems to racism or anxiety, even game development gets thematized. i found each side-story interesting and whilst some characters come off as weird at first, i warmed up to all of them very quickly. in the end, i felt like they started off as strangers but became a small family that is tight-knitted thanks to the café they are all visiting.

brewing coffee
so, the most active part of the player is the process of brewing coffee for their customers. in total, the player has to select three ingredients to produce the coffee. a specific combination is needed for a special kind of coffee, although the customers sometimes just demand simpler versions such as hot or sweet cups. in this case, there is a bar available during the brewing where the player can see the stats for each ingredient. the recipe for each special cup has to be discovered, although the customers are giving the player hints at times.

something that i found very tricky was the latte art for specific drinks. luckily, it's not mandatory and doesn't make any impact on the game, yet it was difficult to create decent latte art. i used that feature around two times before giving up as it takes up a lot of time. anyway, it was still interesting to add that feature so those who are very creative can let off their steam.

in addition to that, there is a "free brew" and "challenge" mode available in coffee talk where the player can either discover new recipes or practice their brewing skills. the free brew mode is pretty simple and allows its player to take their time whilst the challenge one has a time limit so it's important to be fast.

own your own in-game smartphone
so, there is a smartphone available in coffee talk that turned out to be quite useful. the usage of it is entirely optional, however, i loved the features it has to offer and ended up visiting it longer than i assumed i would. in total, it has four applications installed.

the first one is tomodachill. every person the player meets will show up in that application and it kind of reminds me of a reduced version of facebook where the player can read more about the cast's interests. for unlocking more information, it's mandatory that the player gets closer to the character.

the brewpad is probably the most useful application where the player can look up the recipe of all unlocked coffees. i found that was especially helpful in the free brew or challenge mode, especially as it's hard to memorize every recipe.

let's move to the next one, the evening whisperss. as the name already hints at, there are short stories getting released each day that are written by a specific customer. anyway, this was my favorite application as i ended up checking it out every in-game day. the stories are not related at all, yet, i feel like they are still lovely and i had a lot of joy going through each of them.

lastly, there is the shuffld application. this one allows the player to select another soundtrack to listen to, which is a quite nice touch i'd say, although i didn't use it at all.
choices? and what about the endings?
coffee talk doesn't implement choices, however, there are still multiple different endings available in this visual novel. so, the important question is: how is that possible? — well it simply depends on what drinks the player serves their customers. in short: getting them the right drinks does make a huge difference. luckily, the fast forward feature gets unlocked when completing the game once so the player doesn't have to go through the same dialogue again and again. i found it was quite tricky to get everything right during my first playthrough, but luckily it gets easier once i got the gist of it.

graphics and the immersion
graphics-wise, coffee talk is stunning. i always had a soft spot for pixelated styles and this visual novel didn't disappoint either. the thing i loved so much about it is that it's so detailed. for instance, there are windows available in the café where the player can see people passing by and rain falling down. these details made the whole game feel so lively, especially as the characters have multiple facial expressions. as a piece of side information, despite being a visual novel, this game does not contain any cgs besides a few ones at the beginning and end. unfortunately, voice-acting is not present in coffee talk which would have greatly enhanced the immersion.

so, what do we have in the end?
coffee talk is such a lovely and relaxing game i ended up enjoying much more than i anticipated. i liked that this game didn't focus on one storyline but instead shows its reader multiple side-stories and a variety of characters who couldn't be more different. i got attached quickly to each of them and their stories. in addition to that, the process of brewing coffee managed to keep the game refreshing to me. that being said, i can highly recommend coffee talk to everyone who enjoys a cozy game with an excellent cast.

let me clarify something first: i liked the game, but certain aspects of it that i will describe below made my experience with it a mere "...eh...". since steam doesn't have a middle ground on the recomendation buttons, just a yes or no, i have to go with no.
i will now tell you what i went through and therefore what you will probably feel like while playing, just to give my insight on the matter. i will try to be vague enough to not spoil anything.


 the game 

maybe you are here reading the reviews on this game because you got attracted to it's theme, just like me. a dark game where you have to sacrifice homunculi to get your daughter back. sounds awesome! will you get in a dilemma of killing them or not for the sake of a loved one? what would the implications of that be in the main character during the ending?
let's play it!

then you find out that you can't. 
seriously. 
if you wanna progress through the game, you have to kill them. sure, you can just not kill a single one and get one of the endings, but then the game would either be over really soon or you would get stuck in an eternity of repetitive tasks.
just like that, the game became a bit uninteresting for me. but hey, maybe i'm being too judgemental right off the bat. let's play it more so i can get a better idea.


 the gameplay/story 

in the beggining you will be put through the tutorial and the basics of the game. they are intuitive and relatively easy to understand, so no worries there. 
you will also be introduced to our main character. like or dislike him, his story and pursue for his daughter's life is going to be somewhat cativating, which makes the thrive for the development of the plot to be bigger every week. you may find him to be a bit gullible, but you will want to find out the outcome of everything anyway.

however, later you will realize that the gameplay is minimal and extremely repetitive. there is so little you can actually do that sometimes it might feel like a chore. it also is pretty much linear, which kinda dulls the story a little bit. also, since there is no way to progress unless you kill the homunculi, you will probably just get apathetic and simply stop caring about them.
but even though with all these frustrations, you still wanna see how the story develops and how everything ends. 


 the endings 

the true ending will  surely  make you go wait, what???
 i personally think it was a bit crappy. maybe the road that i had to go through to get such and ending intensified that feeling, but i can safely say it could be a lot better.

there are other "game overs" endings in the game, but i heavily discourage for you to go for it in your first playthrough, because they actualy delete your save file (like, really? if you get a "game over" screen, kiss goodbye to all your progress). if you want to go for them first, check a guide and do them in a separate playthrough/save file.

when i finally finished the game and got the true ending, i immediately loaded it again and went for the most obvious bad ending possible in an attempt to complete my diary. even thought i sucessfully got it and made progress in it's completion, going for another load just to find my saved games to be blank really discouraged me. nope, not going through those repetitive mechanics again.


 the veredict 

even though the plot is interesting to an extension and the theme is pretty awesome, the repetitive, linear and annoying gameplay, allied with the somewhat lack of actual content and a pretty meh ending made the game bland. 
in the end, what could be a very freaking awesome game became an average experience.

my final rating would be 5.5/10.

i can only hope that toge productions will take this as a learning experience and step it up for their next game. i absolutely love their previous work and will surely still follow it.

																my lovely daughter is a tricky game to give a simple review to but for the sake of those considering whether or not purchasing it, this is what i think:

this is a game for managing small tasks and routine if you break it down to its most basic level. if you are the kind of person that enjoys games like that, you will easily find yourself having a good time with it. the kinds of games that feel a little bit like work, but in a way that is very laidback. it can be very grindy, but if you find your pace with it you can easily get everything you want from it.

the meat on top of those gameplay bones are the aesthetic and the framing. it is not as story-deep as i would like. that element is there but it leaves quite a bit to be desired? the daughters are really the spotlight of this game. if you like monster girls, there are a lot of them, you get little letters from them throughout the game informing more about how they perceive the world and their personalities. the wiggle room of  how much you'll grow to love and empathize with them varies from person to person, so i suggest seeing maybe a bit of playthrough of this game first and if it interests you, you probably have something to gain from playing this. the art is simple but pleasant enough, not what i would call eye candy but it makes the game stand out a little bit more.

the way it handles its themes though i'm quite mixed about. i'd say this is a game i feel a little uncomfortable thinking about, but not playing. its intent to be offputting is very clear, and i don't feel any maliciousness coming from it, but you will stop caring that you are killing innocent girls, just from a play perspective. it's repetitive enough that it won't impact you after a certain point if it impacts you at all. as someone who was a victim of child abuse, this kind of dark content can be a form of catharsis, but it varies from victim to victim and i would find it completely understandable if this game came across as rather tactless to some. there isn't all that much to meaningfully spoil but the game doesn't make playing from faust's perspective something that has weight. it proposes itself as a game about family and 'how far you'll go for it' which implies a sense of foreboding guilt? but i assure you that you'll never really be able to put yourself into faust's shoes outside of the actual gameplay. 

if you're looking for an in-depth look or for it to have something insightful to say about child abuse, this is not the game you're looking for. if you want a game with elements of child abuse presented in a way that is sympathetic to victims while also not really giving them any way out of the cycle of suffering they're trapped in, this game is it. maybe if you have not been exposed to these scenarios before, it might be a different perspective into the world that you're not used to, and i don't think that's without value, but it doesn't exactly handle them in ways i find extremely helpful for strangers to the subject either. you know. child abuse bad. that's not exactly a very revealing statement. there is more to the text that you can gleam from if you spend a lot of time with it, but it's not something that comes with the experience itself.

in the end, the game only managed to snap me out of numb grind once or twice while reading letters and i felt something for a second and then promptly clicked "kill her", because i "had" to. that's how games are. but i feel it could've been more meaningful and heavier than that. if it's not your type of game then you'll really won't have fun playing it either, nor is it fun to watch. and i don't mean in the sense that this type of game should be entertaining, but it really won't flow for you and you will probably get bored and stop. and there's not a deep deep story hidden in this game that's worth grinding for either. when i type it like this sounds like i didn't like it but also i got to have a bunch of cute daughters whom i loved very much outside of the metanarrative of the game, they were sweet and strong and i'm proud of them, and i'm glad i got to meet all of them by playing this, and they reminded me not only of myself but of my friends who also suffered in the hands of their parents and are still alive today, and while a lot of us feel broken and like monsters, sometimes or a lot of the time, we are all valuable and worthwhile.

so if that resonates with you, maybe give it a shot! may we all be better dads than faust.

																 what is azure saga: pathfinder?
azure saga is a jrpg that feels like it was made by fans of jrpgs instead of a studio with decades of experience like square or atlus. that's fine, of course, it's just something that is worth noting. the story, characters, and world will all feel like familiar takes on the tropes that have defined the genre over the years.

if you're not familiar with jrpgs, essentially you're involved in a grand overarching story filled with really unique characters in a world of nouns you'll not understand until you're more than 1/3rd the way through the game. you'll start out being given names of kingdoms, empires, enemies and friends without much context, but after a few hours of playing it'll all settle in. you'll wander the world, talk to the citizens of the world, and when you delve into dangerous areas, be subject to combat via random encounter.


 what do you do in azure saga? 
typical of the genre, you'll find three of your characters on the left of the screen battling in turn based combat against foes on the right of the screen. your characters will have a variety of abilities available to them, from plain attacks to skills and spells. in addition to this, azure saga carries a system that allows all your characters to attack a single foe in unison. this teamwork feels pretty good once you've figured it out.

later in the game, you'll unlock crafting which will allow you to further customize your characters. the story itself is linear (this is actually typical for the genre and i wouldn't subtract points as other reviews have. after all, the developers have made a linear rpg, it would be unfair to try and say "well it's no skyrim" when it's not trying to be) and the characters carry with them a familiar feeling, thanks to the game feeling more like a love letter to all the best jrpgs of the past.


 azure saga sounds great! any problems? 
on a technical level, the game looks fine, but the asthetic was too "flash game" for me. that's a personal gripe, and the artwork itself is well done, even if it's a style i'm not fond of. the music is actually pretty great and i'd probably buy the soundtrack if they offered it for purchase on steam. while the style isn't a crime, the fact is the game won't be pushing any system to the limit ever. that could be a great thing if you're a gamer that plays on a budget computer.

the tactical depth also isn't what i'm used to from other games in the genre. this too is fine, but for a long time fan of games like this there is likely to be a feeling of "is this it?" from the combat. luckily the story more than makes up for what the combat lacks.

the only true problems i see in the game are from a gameplay design standpoint. they are all problems that any first time developer would have, and masshive media has not made a traditional jrpg game to date, so all these mis-steps are understandable. things like, crafting comes quite late in the game nearly to the point it is useless. the skills lack a certain variety. what little control we have over character development is quite shallow. but the game doesn't feel like a slapped together rpg maker generic clone either.


 do you recommend azure saga? 
i recommend azure saga on the condition you don't mind a story you've heard, characters you've seen, and a world that feels overtly familiar all wrapped around a combat engine that isn't too deep. you are getting 12+ hours of gameplay easily, and while flawed it is enjoyable.

if any part of that sounds like a problem, but you find the game on sale? i'd still recommend picking it up and trying it. if everything sounds like a problem you'd be unable to get past, you might just want to skip it entirely.

																nusakana makes for a nice little island getaway of a game.  it has strengths and weaknesses, and all in all i'd say the pros outweigh the cons.

what's good?
open world to explore at your own pace
eighteen ladies to recruit, each with their own story that progresses as you befriend them
ambush or avoid the local wildlife
characters full of personality
day/night cycle and weather patterns
survivalist mechanics including hunger and sleep deprivation
multiple game modes that affect mechanics and difficulty
handy in-game encyclopedia that adds information as you discover it
what are the problems?
game gets easier instead of more challenging as you progress
main plot is poorly paced with underwhelming resolution
learning weapon skills is mindlessly repetitive
loads of engrish (aside from when it's meant to be poorly spoken in dialogue)
fishing at sea is easy to glitch into softlocking
fishing gameplay lacks depth and challenge
basically, the idea is you've come to a remote tropical island because someone sent you a letter saying they could reveal to you your mysterious past (you were raised in foster care and never knew your parents).  starting as a dumb tourist, you learn to live on the island and slowly become a familiar and admired fixture in the native community.  you forage and hunt for food and crafting materials, get paid for fulfilling requests posted across four request boards, camp in the wilderness, and meet and befriend girls ranging from little kids to mature women.

you can have up to three ladies accompanying you at any given time--one fights beside you in battle and the other two provide support effects unique to each character.  you can equip them with accessories, and eventually power up their swimsuits/armor to your preferred specifications.  they also automatically learn certain weapon skills that you unlock for yourself.

the game is at it's hardest when you're just starting out, with basically no money, no decent equipment, and wildlife that can tear you a new one.  then, once you figure out how to make a bunch of money, the game's difficulty evaporates.



all in all, when you play this game, you play it to explore the island, soak in the atmosphere, and get to know the girls, all at whatever pace you feel.  don't worry too much about the main excuse plot or being heavily challenged and play the game like it's a big playground for adventure.

																insurgence rpg is an rpgmakermv game created by an indonesian game developer. a lot of indonesians might like the game a lot, but it’s still good for people around the world, too. first of all, i’ve played the pre-release version of the game for 15 hours (7 hours logged in, 6 hours on offline mode, 2 hours slacking off). also, i have not played many rpgmaker games myself, but i will state what i know based on my limited experience.

short review: pros:
+ intriguing story about political intrigue… nuff said.
+ considerably balanced difficulty
+ interesting attribute weakness/strength system
+ decent graphics
+ cg arts are a good addition
+ awesome music
+ some indonesian cultural references
+ fair amount of content with dirt cheap price
+ good devs response

cons:
- a lot of grammatical errors
- some scenes were rushed
- some sprites are standard rpgmaker ones

neutral:
= your typical rpgmaker game
= standard battle system
= ui design is good, but the icon layout did not feel intuitive at first
= full controller support, but with minimal guidance for keyboard users

in-depth review
story
the game tells a story about political intrigue. basically, there was an evil plot devised by someone in a certain kingdom, and it’s up to the main character (who is the princess) to stop them. to start, the princess was tasked to hunt the leader of a rebellious faction. and then the adventure began… that may look like your standard jrpg story, but it is actually deeper than that. i will say no further though, to prevent any kind of spoilers.

the plot is nice and well thought out, though the only and the most lacking of all would be the writing. some grammatical errors also persist on the release version. this might be due to the lack of a good editor fluent in english on the developer side. however, the mistakes are mostly minor, so i think it will not leave a major impact to the story. 
in the pre-release version, there were some rushed scenes which will leave you, as the player, speechless. i have not checked whether this is still true in the release version though, but i will leave this here nonetheless.

gameplay
like many rpgmaker games out there, you will play a turn-based rpg (but with more tactical options). the action order is shown though, so you can plan more thoroughly than many other rpgmaker games. 
there are also 3 types of attack, normal attack which recovers 10 tp, magic attack which requires mp to cast but does not recover tp, and special attack which uses tp. there are also 2 types of healing items. one can be used inside combat, and the other is non-combat exclusive. 

lastly, the game has a hidden attribute weakness/strength system which is kinda different from other rpg games. for instance, you may think that fire is weak to water, but in this game this is not the case. fire is both strong and weak to ice but neutral to water. so if you cast a fire spell on an ice enemy, it will deal a strong damage, and if you cast an ice spell on a fire enemy it will also deal a strong damage. however you will deal normal damage to water, and minimal damage to fire enemies. in short, fire >><< ice, fire ==== water, fire …. fire (hopefully this is understandable lol).

those 3 types of attacks, 2 types of items, and attribute weakness/strength system need to be utilized wisely to move on, since tp is limited to 100 for each character and they do not have much mp to cast spells anytime. however, if you are a veteran to turn-based rpgs i’m sure you’ll know all about those intuitively.

on the matter of difficulty, if you have played similar turn-based rpg before, normal difficulty is the good place to start. you can even go to hard mode instead if you prefer more challenge. on the pre-release version even the hard mode was so easy that i’ve beaten the final boss in less than a minute, but thankfully the developer addressed the issue and rebalanced the game.

but if you just wanna enjoy the story, normal or lower is recommended.

graphics
well, some tilesets and npc sprites are the ones you can see in every rpgmaker game, but let’s forget about that, and talk about the original ones.

for the character design, i think it’s decent. they use anime-style character graphics, so for those turned off by anime, this game might not be for you. however, they are unlike those overly exaggerated anime characters using, like, absurd huge weapons, cute colorful costumes, cringe dialogues, etc. they all seemed… normal to me, which is a good thing.

the ui graphics is also good enough. pretty simple, but still good. it reminds me of tales of berseria ui graphics, though…. the only downside was that the way icons are laid out on the menu felt so confusing at first. another thing i like was that there’s

there are also some cg arts to collect throughout the game. some of them are good, while some others are not so. 
there is also another matter about the graphics, but i will say it on the following section.

sound & music
i think the strongest aspect of the game is the soundtrack that i’ve never even once get bored of them. the battle themes are so immersive, especially the boss themes. they might not be at nihon falcom’s or nier’s soundtrack level, but at least they are immersive and very enjoyable. the only thing that i don’t like was the music that played on sad scenes, it felt so out of place to me. 

i also like the opening and ending themes, in which the singer was fleurishana. if you’re not an indonesian, you may not heard of her though. too bad the opening movie was low in frame rate and (perhaps) in not so good resolution though.

controls
i have played the game both using a logitech f710 wireless controller and a keyboard, and i have not found any issues. there are different kinds of issue, though: even if you are using a keyboard, the interface is still showing xbox controller input buttons. also, there are some functions which are not explicitly stated iirc. that is, using lb/rb, pgup/pgdn or q/e for cycling through characters on a menu, pressing ? button for skipping a turn in battle, and ? button for an extra option (retreat). 

others
the game is created by an indonesian developer, so expect a lot of indonesian cultural references being laid out here and there. just like those japanese games which add a lot of japanese cultural references. the references are mostly about indonesian foods, others are indonesian jokes. if you are familiar with them, you will like those immediately, but if you don’t, you will not get them though.

overall
when i was playing the pre-release version, i guessed that the price would be around $10. but to my surprise, it is actually half of that. the game has a good amount of content, despite being an rpgmaker game, so i think the game deserves more than $5. the game has a good story, gameplay,  and music, after all. but i guess it’s a win-win both for the devs and the players, so eh, why not. for the price of a burger which you will consume in less than 10 minutes, you will get 10 hours amount of gameplay! it’s a steal, if i may say so myself.

the game indeed has a lot of flaws, and many of them are not stated in my review. but judging by the game, it seems the dev will be developing another, or maybe some more games. i’m sure the future games will be much better, so i’m looking forward to it. the devs also seems to be highly responsive of feedbacks and bug reports so that’s a huge positive in my book.

with all those, i’ll give an overall score of 6 out of 10 for this game.

the brewing minigame is an interesting touch to give the game some gameplaymechanics.

i was interested in the characters, but not invested. most of them have zero to none character development besides "quiet at first but then started talking" - which might be reasoned with the very short play time of 5 hours, which is tough considering they have to introduce a lot of characters, their problems, and how they manage to overcome them. 
there just isnt enough time for more complex characters or problems. 

any bonus runs require around one hour to skip through all of it and read any previously unseen messages - and the difference is mostly just a short text after the credits.

however, i encountered major issues in all 3 runs i did - the first run was standard, i did somethings right, some things wrong, your average first blind run. but characters suddenly said things i had no clue of - in the perfect run, my second one, i realized that characters only told certain things if you give them the right drink.

but why on earth does the rest of the game act like they said a certain thing, even though it never happened?
it is a 5 hour game with very few things that can go in a different way - and not including different options if a character said something or not was a disappointment to discover. and a little bit confusing the first run.

worldbuilding is something i'd say is necessary in these "service novels" as i like to call them. the immersion is expanded upon by magnitudes. in va-11 you could browse danger/u/, read kira miki's blog, and more. the most worldbuilding we get in coffee talk is through natural dialogue and the little segment of news you get at the start of a day. in-dialogue worldbuilding is done very well, however outside of it, there is very little to supplement our knowledge of this fantasy-like place. 

in terms of mechanics, i think that coffee talk has wonderful ways to depict a drink's properties with 4 bars of different qualities, as well as providing you with very good feedback in regards to drink design. most of the drinks in the earlier part of the game are things you can figure out by yourself within the given 5 tries, and you only need to dig deeper into the dialogue transcript. i only have a small issue in regards to the order of ingredients in drinks. often times, your solution for a drink may be right under your nose - you only need to swap primary and secondary ingredients. this can, and has lead to frustration before. 

as a tiny side note from a barista: i think that the latté art mechanic is super interesting, albeit it could use more work. i quite enjoyed playing around with it!

tl;dr with va-11 hall-a comparisons:
the game is a very short experience (5 hours max) that conveys aesthetics and story in the same way that va-11 did without heavy worldbuilding, with less immersion and more focus on in-the-moment situations, rather than overarching plots.

one of my all time favorite games is va-11 hall-a and ever since, i’ve been on the lookout for similar games ever since to scratch that itch it left behind. the closest i’ve gotten was playing the red strings club which does have you literally pouring drinks to bring out certain emotions in your customers, but it turned out to be disappointing (for me at least). when i heard about coffee talk though, i knew i was going to pick this one up and play it as soon as i could. my decision was hammered home even more after i played the demo. well, now that coffee talk is released how does it fare?

taking place in seattle in an alternate 2020, you find yourself in a world that hosts not only humans but fantasy creatures like mermaids and elves. though, that doesn’t mean this world doesn’t have it’s own set of problems. that is where you come in as the owner, and only employee, of a small coffee shop named coffee talk. what sets yours out from all the others is that yours is the only one that is open only at night. ready for anyone to come in looking for a hot drink and an ear to air out all their frustrations.

coffee talk’s cast of characters are wonderful as each bring in their own unique personality to the table and stories on what’s currently happening in their lives. each one manages to interesting to where most players will want to hear more about them and hope that they’ll come in before you close up. you’ll start out with freya, a regular that always comes in to write and is aspiring to have a book published. it’s not long before you meet up with an elf and succubus couple that’s struggling with their families not approving their relationship and what the future holds if they never do; a cop that’s totally not taking too many breaks to have a cup of your coffee; a vampire model that gives insight on and to whoever happens to be there; a werewolf that’s trying to find a drink that will calm him down during his fury; and more. you also have some other world building elements through daily newspapers (headlines only sadly), tomodachill profiles that opens up more information as you get closer to the characters, and you’re even able to read some of freya’s short stories to give you a taste on how she writes.

brewing up drinks for your customers is pretty simple. at first you’ll only have a couple ingredients, but you’ll slowly get more as inventory comes in. you’ll pick a base, a primary ingredient, and finally a secondary ingredient. while you’ll brew the usual drinks like espressos, lattes, and flavored milk, there are also special named drinks you can discover and customers will occasionally request. however, you won’t have the full list, only having the basics already in your brewpad, as you’re meant to discover them yourself. as some customers will request named drinks, with some giving hints and others not, it also means you most likely won’t be able to give everyone correct drinks. luckily, coffee talk doesn’t change anything other than them saying it’s not what they ordered apart from two instances. these two instances are telegraphed so it’s not hidden away if you’re worried about that.

for lattes, coffee talk also lets you create your own latte art if you wanted to. i personally found it hard to make anything, well, pleasing. basically the long you hold own, the more milk will be poured and it’ll be pushed down. if you don’t like it when you try it out, you can completely ignore it.

coffee talk also features an endless mode with two different choices. first, you have free brew which lets you make anything. this is mainly used to let you figure out all named drink combinations as you won’t be able to make all of them in your first playthrough or be able to figure it out if you’re not given any hints. then there’s challenge mode. challenge mode, well, challenges you to make as many correct drinks as you can for your customer before the time runs out. each correct drink adds on more time so you can survive longer. it starts out pretty easy with them just saying what ingredients they want outright. it slowly brings up the difficulty as it brings your base to the end of their request and occasionally requesting a named drink (that you hopefully discovered before now). lastly, it gets more vague on what ingredients they want, but more specific on how they want sweet, warm, cool, or bitter they want their drink to be. this is where it gets challenging as it first starts with only requesting one aspect to be a certain way to all of them. though, this part is a bit confusing at first before you figure out what the customer actually means. asking for a drink that’s not bitter and extra sweet is obvious, but what about less and just regular sweet. especially when they just plainly say “i want my drink to be bitter” and they hate it when you just load it up. well, you might not have noticed, but the coffee maker actually tells you what constitutes as a drink having a low or high amount in each. 1-3 bars is less, 4-5 is just right, and 6+ is extra. when the game asks for a normal amount of one of them, it will only accept 4-5 as anything more counts as it being too much.

when you think of a game centering around being a barista, i would be surprised if the first thing on your mind wasn’t a cozy coffee shop where you can go and study or write. coffee talk certainly doesn’t disappoint if you’re expecting a cozy atmosphere. the coffee shop just shouts cozy vibes with how it’s decorated, the characters are wonderfully designed and brings in a pop of vividity, the soundtrack is relaxing and i could easily see them being in a “relaxing cafe music for studying” playlist, and the rain certainly brings in another addition for those that find rain relaxing.

this game definitely reminds me of a 10 hour rainy mood loop of beneath the mask that i listen to sometimes while i write so i’m not writing in complete silence. combining a relaxing soundtrack with the sound of rain pouring down outside and the image of you just sitting in a coffee shop watching people walk and drive by the window.

one thing i do wish was that coffee shop was a bit longer. not because the price doesn’t fit, which i do think it does, but it felt like there could have been more interactions between the characters. while these things didn’t bother me much, others might be disappointed that giving wrong drink orders doesn’t really affect anything outside two separate instances and it doesn’t show the complexity of brewing coffee. the latter is a shame as i would have been interested in learning about it, especially since i even looked up how baristas make latte art in an effort to understand how the latte art minigame worked.

verdictwhile coffee talk might not completely scratch that itch that va-11 hall-a left in many of it’s players, it will satisfy those that have been looking for similar games. while it can disappoint in some areas, it gives players a wonderful cast of characters, a cozy atmosphere to relax to, two endings, and a challenge mode for those who are looking for a challenge.

---------------------------------

gameplay-wise, the game is very similar to clash royale in the sense that you'll be playing your cards in real-time as the mana bar below is constantly being refilled. your opponent will do the same. units will automatically follow the path, much like a creep does in a moba, but in this game, you'll get to switch the signposts to direct your units onto the path you want. there are also more "structures" you can and should destroy (usually) along each path as opposed to having only the final castle at the end of the path like in clash royale. in some ways, these structures are like the towers in a moba game but if you do manage to destroy them, you'll get a nice mana regen boost.

for me, the game is very addictive and fun at the beginning, though i guess some people might feel like the game's too easy at that point. i've managed to get to sector 3 on my first run, which is a personal best. i only lost sector 3 mainly because my deck is spell-heavy and i was severely penalized for that. 

however, after that first run, my character leveled up to level 4, and unlocked a deck and some new cards which i don't get access to from the get-go. this is where the balancing of the game became an issue. the ai has some insane relics that gave them massive boosts while i'm still playing like i'm in level 1. i felt that i was severely handicapped and i wouldn't be wrong. 

pros+ really challenging, yet addictive and fun, gameplay after your first defeat. before, my character is still level 1 and the battles seem rather easy... not that i'm complaining :p
+ short sessions per sector - around the same amount of time needed to finish a moba match.
+ 3 unique characters with very different playstyles and decks
+ nice progression system where you'll get to unlock (and only unlock) more powerful cards or new starter decks the more your hero levels up. 
+ mobile-like graphics that look good here. i actually quite like the card art and the game map as well! 
+ some randomization which makes every playthrough with the same character slightly different. 

cons/feedback- glitches - enemies getting stuck; cards that don't do as stated (the archers; i had both versions - an upgraded one with longer range and one with normal range. i sent them out at almost the same time, but they both stood in the same position when they fire projectiles at the enemy)
- the game seems to push you towards building a well-rounded deck. lean towards any one side and the game will penalize you heavily, eventually. 
- leveling up a character seems to penalize the player somehow. enemies end up starting off with much stronger units and insane buffs while i don't.
- balancing is a major issue here. i've encountered games where the ai has insane relics that basically forced me to play my deck the way it's not supposed to be played, while i can do nothing to hamstring my opponent.
- game froze for a bit in my third stream. i thought the game crashed.
- the game isn't in early access but it has many issues that are often associated with a game being in early access. to put it simply, necronator: dead wrong isn't ready for release.

overallat the moment, i would not recommend buying necronator: dead wrong unless it is on a steep discount. the game still needs a lot of work and it just feels like the game was forced out of the womb before it's ready. however, if you've seen the gameplay in action and loved every moment of it, then i would definitely recommend wishlisting it and checking in now and then. there's something really special here and the game does have lots of potential; it's just that the game is marred by, mainly, balancing issues and glitches, which i hope would be fixed some time soon.

																an extremely chill and relaxing brewing game ?
coffee talk, surprisingly, is not like any other brewing games which you have always play or seen. it is a sort of visual novel game where you play as the proprietor and the only barista of a coffee shop in an alternate version of seattle. it’s still 2020, and it still rains every day, but the world is also full of magical creatures. your patrons include not only humans, but also vampires, elves, werewolves, mermaids, and other mythical beings. 

each day starts the same. you will get to read the headlines of the local paper, the evening whisperer, to get a sense of the state of the world before opening the shop. there’s a regular, freya, a journalist who spends her evenings in the cafe struggling to write a novel. but for the most part, you don’t know what to expect when the front door opens and someone steps in. it could be a budding pop star who is stressed out by her overprotective father, an orc game developer in the midst of exhausting crunch, or maybe an elf and succubus whose families won’t accept their relationship. you might even be accosted by a government agent who is just looking for a literal alien. all the characters are pretty quirky and fantastical. most of the time, your job is to simply sit and listen. they start out as strangers, but you’ll naturally grow close to them over time. 

i love the concept on how we are able to step into the role of a barista, creating drinks and interacting with customers, revolve in a world where humans and fantastical creatures co-exist. what i love most is how the game also trying to convey numbers of philosophical issues such as racism; for example how freya stated that even if we are living in the world where only humans exist, they will still try to find every little small details to draw a line.

the pixel-art visuals are definitely awesmazing - it gives the game a personality, and the character designs are very imaginative, especially for the orc game designer and nekomimi popstar.  all the elements in this game — from endearing writing to the soothing soundtrack — they are all beautifully blend together to create such a supremely chill experience. the stories may be serious, but the experience is mellow. there are no time limits or any game over screens to deal with, so there will be no pressure to enjoy this game.

personally, i feel that this is one of the most relaxing gameplay i ever had. i definitely would love to see more of indie games such as this one appear more often. overall, this is a pretty worthy game to play and it really leave quite an impression in my mind. thank you so much for the game. i love it so much that it truly hold a special place in my heart.

the gameplay follows the classic jrpg model, with a global map where all discovered locations are displayed, locations divided in sections (squares, in this case), containing items, chests, secrets, fishing spots, and quest-giving npcs. some parts of locations will not be accessible at first, but only later as parts of various quests. many locations will be mandatory for the main storyline, but some are optional and will lead to secret bosses and quests. 

in asp, you will find a less in-depth customization of character than many other jrpgs, as the only equipment that can be changed are two pieces of armor, and two attachable jewels, categorized clearly in items more oriented for support, mage, tank, so your choices in what to equip to who will be pretty clear to make. jewels can activate additional armor proprieties if they are the correct type. there also are no level-up choices, attributes or anything like that, completely automatic in that sense.

combat is turn-based, all the allies will act in the same turn, and then all the enemies. there is a system of weaknesses / resistances of certain enemy types to certain ability types, or damage types, basic statuses such as stun, poison, silence, taunt and so on. there also is a system called fury, charging a special attack bar the more damage your characters sustain, to then unleash a powerful attack with unique effects. one of the unique mechanics consists in the unity attacks special moves that can be discovered by attacking in the same turn with a precise order of character skills. there are 50 combinations to be discovered, each with unique effects and powers. 

overall, i found asp a decent jrpg, that could use improvements especially in quality of life, the story is pretty cliche and you will get a hint of what really happened from the beginning, but that doesn't mean it's bad at all. quests are often fetch or kill quests without particular interest, and frankly they are rarely worth doing, plus, a special mention must be done to the last level, which i a total game design disaster and results in a very annoying and frustrating experience. so much that it prevented me from finishing it, in fact.

 gameplay analysis 

 general gameplay 
gameplay is mainly divided into exploration and combat. exploration is done in real-time in an isometric map, and features some puzzles to solve from time to time, fetching keys and elements to progress in levels, getting quests and rewards from npcs, and loot from chests. fishing is also a thing and is a nice simple mini-game to pass some time and get some fish as consumable, to use in battle.

an arena is also unlocked at a certain point, featuring challenging encounters and unique rewards for those who are brave enough. some additional progression elements are uncovered later on, such as tattoos, used to specialize further your team members, and also gem fusion, to fuse gems of the same type and rank in more powerful versions. crafting is also a thing, usable at crafting benches found in various levels, but it is not very useful to be honest.

to buy all these things you will need money, dropped from monsters, or gained from chests or quests sometimes. in the game's first half money will be an issue, but then later it won't.


 story 
the story is a bit predictable, but good enough to keep you entertained. it is not particularly over the top, or well written, but not bad either. average.

 combat system 
combat is turn-based like in most jrpgs, the only unique mechanics being the fury system and the unity attack mechanic. enemies will have weaknesses to specific abilities and types of damage, as will your characters. classes are clearly divided into dps, support, tank and so on, with abilities to match these roles. enemies willa swell have fury abilities (but not united) and unleash them when the time comes, often only bosses have them though.

a better explanation of vulnerabilities, status duration, and effects would be good, as often it is not exactly clear what is weak to which attacks, and why. other than this, a pretty solid classic jrpg combat system, even if quite simplistic if compared to other titles.

 content & pricing 
priced at 13€, and lasting a good 25-30 hours if you are aiming to complete every optional boss, secret quest etc, i'd say this game has a good content price ratio. a good deal.

 balancing & challenge 
some bosses can literally stun-lock / silence-lock entire parties without specific items / builds, making such battles very cheesy. luckily most of these are optional ones. nothing apart from this.



 technical analysis 

 graphics 
well done 2d hand-drawn style, animations and effects. artistically, asp has a very good eye-candy for an indie title and hits the mark in depicting the world it is set into.

 sound 
average soundtracks and effects, without particular praise.

 performance & stability 
nothing to report. solid.

 ai 
enemy ai will generally be tied to their specific class: support units will heal and buff, dps will attack viciously, tanks will do their job, stunning and crippling enemies. overall a good ai for a jrpg.

 quality of life 
there are many problems here. quest items are not displayed on the map even if you visited the room they are located in, so if a player misses them, he will spend hours roaming maps to try and find some key or bauble to open a door. arena battles do not heal party if victorious. players cannot certainly escape a battle if they wish to do so, but it's chance based. levels with much weaker monsters will still trigger encounters and make players lose a lot of time for no reason. quest items cannot be picked up if the quest for them has not been taken, forcing players to huge backtracking. 

 bugs / issues 
the issues mentioned above make the last game level a very frustrating and not fun experience, i personally spent 5 hours roaming that single dungeon in search of a quest item, but since it was not displayed, i gave up, and spent tons of resources in the process because of unskippable encounters all the time. a very sour drink in an otherwise pleasant experience. this was the only major issue with the game.


 conclusion & rating azure saga pathfinder is a decent jrpg, with problems in quality of life that impair it a bit, and a complete disaster in level design regarding the last stage. still, i suggest it to jrpg fans as it is pretty good overall, but mind my words, you will get angry at the last stage!

graphics are better, as they should. not the best, but it's very beautiful. there are graphical glitches with the occlusion culling (i believe i'm talking about the right thing). some angles may make the game "un render" the image, and also the cellphone camera may not capture the lod, showing only what is near. aside from those, no problems.

i must say the game doesn't focus on scares, it's more tension, exploration and unfolding the story rather than showing a horror time.

i truly enjoyed this game, another masterpiece. it is slow on some times, and also have lots of action, but if you want only action, you may find that the game is short and boring. if you immerse yourself in it, then you can enjoy the experience for real :)

if you're asking yourself why it's frustrating:
the game has some rough edges that can actually hurt you physically. jk
this kind of game is cool to be played straight. dying a lot or having to restart can kill the mood easily.
in 2 areas, the character entered a place where she couldn't get back, so i had to restart.
the lack of direction and hold handing is much welcome, but some things should be adjusted for the players to have a better experience.

you'll probably need some patience if you play casually. most horror games can be played casually, and dying a lot cuts half of the fun.
sadly, in dreadout 2 the hitbox for the phone camera is not exactly what you think it is. aim for the head, not the body. and it must be on the center of the camera. and at the exact time.
you can't dodge, but you also can't take quick shots. if it is going to hit you, forget it and take your damage. it's mostly ok after you get the momentum, but even so you can't see the ghost, it appears too close and the photo doesn't hit, even with you taking a nice picture of the ghost.

frustrating, but you can do it.
one of the bosses is actually bugged, hitting you from nowhere and after it alread missed an attack.
you can also lock youself on walls and die a miserable death without a chance to get away from enemies.

because linda is slow. she can walk fast, ok, but she takes too much time to take a picture or to activate the flash, meaning sometimes you'll be stuck getting hit while not being able to stun or attack the enemy back.
good thing is, i noticed some of these problems from begining to mid game. from mid to late game, it felt much better to fight, things happened as they should, ghosts acted as they should, etc. the final acts are all smooth to play.
not talking about difficulty, but reaction time.

oh, i played it in english. most characters and scenes do not have voice, only subtitles. most voice lines are not 'translated', they speak in the mother language of the game. important characters were dubbed. i don't think it is a problem at all, but i think it's worth noting, since some may think it is of poor quality because of that alone. it is not.

it's worth every cent, even with the rough edges.

again, 11/10.
good work dh, hope you keep making amazing games,

																quick summary for anyone who is familiar with va-11 hall-a, as coffee talk derives a lot of inspiration from it.

is it very similar to va-11 hall-a? yes.
is it as good as va-11 hall-a? no.
is it still enjoyable? yes.

for a short summary of the game itself, coffee talk is a slice-of-life game set in modern-day seattle, with the addition of classic fantasy races like elves and vampires. the game takes place over a few days at the same coffee shop, where customers interact and you learn about their lives. the story itself doesn't have the traditional beginning and end; rather, it takes place in the middle, with an indeterminate beginning and an indeterminate end.

the characters are...decently written. none of them are overly annoying, and i ended up liking all of them, but most of them ended up not having a ton of depth to them. the real shame is that the character who is in the shop the most was among the least interesting among the customers. again, she's not unlikable, but i didn't find her particularly deep or compelling. this is actually one of the two chief problems with the game - wanting more - which i'll touch on later.

probably the largest problem is that the shop itself felt weirdly disconnected from the rest of the world. it almost felt like another dimension, where nothing that happened out in the world affected the shop in any way. while i can appreciate the escapism of such an approach, it also means that it's hard to have any real stake in the world that's been created. the characters seem to have no real place in it. no more apparent is that than in the choice of the barista you play as. they are genderless and faceless, and are in effect an extension of you. this again creates a disconnect as you can't really provide clear explanations as to why the barista does what they do, as the only real decisions you make in the game come from whether or not you serve customers the correct drinks (and what, if anything, you draw on their lattes). as you learn after completing the main story, there is a small twist concerning the identity of said barista, but the revelation is not worth the buildup and easily could have been discarded entirely. va-11 hall-a's bartender, jill, was an everywoman with a clear identity and a place in the world, and as such was easily relatable. unfortunately, that's not the case here.

the other issue with the game is, admittedly, not inherently a bad thing: i was left wanting more. the days felt very short. while there is an endless mode to dabble in, in 4 hours i completed the entire main story, including the aforementioned twist. part of the problem may well have had to do with the setting: characters getting multiple alcoholic beverages in a bar - and staying longer and being more open - makes sense, while getting multiple coffees doesn't. regardless, the days kept moving and as such, the characters didn't have enough time to develop. they all had their basic arc with a conflict to resolve, and that was it.

it's a solid effort, and as i said, wanting more is not inherently a bad thing: i wanted more investment in the world and the characters in it, as there was a lot of potential here. unfortunately, i didn't get it, but i did ultimately enjoy the experience, and as such i still recommend it, especially if you've gone through va-11 hall-a. it's kind of like spaghetti without the sauce: it's close to what you want, and it gets the job done, but it's not quite what you're looking for.

			andy reviews indie horror dating sim, my lovely daughter.		
	

do you remember how in assassin's creed brotherhood, you had to raise up your own little team of assassin cub scouts, sending them off on missions and watching their stats grow? imagine, if you will, that you found out, halfway through the game, that you were, in fact, training them up so that the assassin order could send them off to do kamikaze dives with those rickety da vinci gliders. imagine further, that instead of burly italian thugs and saucy wenches, your squad of renaissance suicide bombers was being recruited from innocent ten-year-old girls.  

that's the position we find ourselves placed in by my lovely daughter, a crafting/relationship sim, out this year from gamechanger studios. 
upon starting the game, we find ourselves in the shoes of an amnesiac alchemist, unimaginatively named faust. the game's primary challenge is then quite efficiently presented to us, in the form of an empty house, a magic book, and a dead daughter.
as faust, we quickly learn that in order to revive our dead daughter we must infuse her preserved soul with those harvested from home-made little monster-girls called homunculi. each homunculus has a single emotional stat, which has to be groomed in order to make them effective sacrifices. this is achieved by sending them off to do jobs in the neighboring village, and by giving them presents. at the same time, we have to make sure that our artificial children don't run away before we can murder them, and that our daughter's body doesn't decompose, before we figure out how to resurrect her. 
the game interface reminds one strongly of those newgrounds point-and-click flash games from the early 2000s, and the art style reminds one of a webcomic from the same era. that flash game attitude carries on into the gameplay, which largely consists of acquiring resources and seeing what you can combine them into, and the affection and personality measures are reminiscent of those flash rpg dating sims, where you have to court each character according to their one personality trait.

the concept is kind of interesting, though. the process of raising up your home full of nightmarish little digipets is lent some extra weight by the fact that the game will eventually force you to kill them. the minimalistic approach means that you won't constantly be interrupting the experience to look at walkthroughs. the stylized animation is capable of delivering some genuinely striking imagery, while avoiding the slip into sleazy torture porn.

on the flip-side, though, the limited number of game mechanics means that it tends to drag on a bit, and the impact of the imagery quickly gets lost in the sheer drudgery of the stat management.  despite the interesting concept, the storytelling is kind of weak, too. the only scripted events seem to occur at the beginning and end of the game, and the game world isn't reactive enough to allow for any kind of an emergent story, along the way.  

this is a game that i think might have benefited from being formatted more like a conventional adventure game. you'd lose a some of the autonomy in the gameplay, but as it stands, the game doesn't really have the story structure that its highbrow concept is crying out for. 

you see, in the mythology of this game, the homonculi are a bit like blade runner's replicants: it's left open to what extent these artificial creations are real people. the game takes some serious effort to characterize them, and makes a point of the fact that the development of their personalities is necessary to faust's plan. buried in the premise is the idea that each homonculus gets closer to becoming a fully realized, conscious individual, as they get closer to their inevitable death at the protagonist's hands. that could set up a pretty serious moral dilemma, asking the audience to consider what constitutes a sentient life, and whether one life can genuinely be more important than another. 

the only problem with that, is that the game seems to be completely insensitive to the issue, as does our main character. he never shows even a scrap of remorse over killing his creations, and his regard for any for the human characters begins and ends with worrying about them interfering with his evil scheme. 

ironically, --because it seems to be an accident-- the game isn't a bad exploration of a certain kind of evil. faust has an objective that he thinks is justified, and as far as he's concerned, everyone else is either a tool or an obstacle toward that goal. through his perspective, the line between the homonculi and the human characters is irrelevant. he regards everyone not himself as an object, and that's about as good a definition of evil as i can think of. 

so what we have here is a game in which you play as what is unquestionably the villain, an interesting concept in itself, but without a hero to offset you, the game's moral universe feels incomplete. consequently, while the ambience of the game can be unsettling, the story lacks much in the way of a satisfying payoff. 

the lack of a more structured story leads to some other missed opportunities, too. there's never much of a sense of threat in this game. yeah, if you fail to buy a preservative for your daughter's corpse, it will deteriorate and eventually lead to game a game over, but the item necessary is in infinite supply at the shop,  and i never found myself short on cash. the bigger mistake is that there doesn't seem to be any chance of the villagers catching on to what you're up to. another thing this game is crying out for is a "young frankenstein"-esque nosy police inspector, to periodically come poking around and asking questions. 

without wishing to spoil, the endings aren't up to much, either. particularly the "true" ending, which throws the established tone overboard with a ham-fisted analogy about becoming trapped in a spiral of negative behavior.  

gamechanger's self-declared intent, at least as far as can be inferred from the game's -- frankly pretentious -- steam page,  is to use the game as an exploration of a variety of personal and social ills, including "child labor, abusive parenting, and ignorant societies". on that level, its an unmitigated failure, just because every single character is so one-dimensionally miserable and depressing, that any attempt at social commentary is hard to take seriously. it's also claiming to be a serious portrayal of grief, but the protagonist isn't much deeper than the average mad scientist, and he never seems to undergo any kind of emotional change or development. 

in fact, after playing the game, the steam page for it is starting to remind me of the information cards at modern art exhibits: desperately trying to preemptively convince you that if you don't like it, it's just too artistic and serious for you. 

would i recommend it? well, it's certainly a more clever subversion of its genre than doki doki literature club, but it also isn't free. my lovely daughter isn't as disturbing as the developers clearly think it is, and it's not terribly immersive, either. the game sucked me in initially, but the repetitive nature of its slow-paced, and sometimes obscure management gameplay will probably undercut your investment in the story. the concept is worthwhile, and it'll be plenty different from anything else on your steam list, but there just isn't enough game here to carry it for me.

in this day of steam sales and free downloads, it seems a little gutsy to me, to charge $15 for what is essentially a glorified flash game, especially when you can get most of the experience from watching a few youtube videos. but i also have to admit that i don't like crafting games or relationship sims, so your mileage may vary. if you like that kind of thing, you'll have to decide if the concept is worth the money to you.

posted: december 9, 2019
																so, another day, another retro-style jrpg. this one's aping the ps1/ps2 era, it seems - with the setting invoking star ocean: the second story in particular. advanced spacefuture hero crashes on comparatively primitive sword-and-sorcery world, is inexplicably good with a sword, adventure happens. not a bad setup, really. the gameplay is the most basic kind of turn-based rpg-combat - all your guys take turns hitting, then all the bad guys take turns hitting, and it just goes like that. throw in chrono trigger-style combination-attacks (sort of) and some virtually mandatory 'limit break' style moves, and you get a jrpg soup that, while perhaps not likely to excite your palate with new and novel spices, at least promises to be filling - and it comes with that warm sensation of nostalgia we all love. oh, i suppose there's a bit of originality on display - literally, since the only thing that really makes you go "huh, you don't see that very often..." is the graphics. the game is built around a rather novel 'paperdoll' style which... is hard to describe, but then, there are videos right up there you can watch. either way, 's a nice touch.
so why the negative review, you ask? well, two things, really. firstly, the technical side. the game feels rather... poorly optimized. it's hard to really put your finger on it, but the controls don't feel as sharp as they ought, and whenever you're running around a dungeon, you have a persistent feeling that the camera is lagging behind somehow. there's also plenty of glitches - small stuff, mostly, like half the scenery blinking in and out of existence, but there are supposedly also far nastier stuff around, according to what i've seen on the board. can't say anything about that myself, of course, since i haven't gotten that far. 
the real kicker is the other thing, though - the writing. it's just... laughably terrible. just... so, so, so bad. and in a jrpg, that matters. far from feeling believable or fleshed-out, the characters you meet seem to switch randomly between being grateful and awed at your heroic deeds, being arrogantly disdainful of this no-name vagrant who thinks he can just go around talking to high priestesses and kings, or just numbly going through the motions of handing out the quests that the medium demands. the way people act and react makes no sense whatsoever. i think the quality on display here is best encapsulated by this exchange early on in the game, paraphrased just a touch...

synch, the hero who wields the high-tech plasma-sword: quiet, my loyal android follower! these people are clearly using medieval-level tech. we must have somehow stumbled into a primitive human civilization, even though they speak the exact same language we do, without any noticeable linguistic drift. we must carefully hide our space-future origins!
noide, an android with visible, external, mechanical components and glowing eyes: yes sir.
clery, a priestess from a medieval civilization, as noide decimates enemies with twin revolvers and summons a hover-drone to analyze them: my, it certainly is peculiar how these strangers are unfamiliar with the monsters and magical weather that are common throughout this kingdom...

i may have taken a few liberties with the wording, but that's basically exactly how it goes. actually, why is an android servant from a remote space-future wielding a pair of revolvers in the first place, instead of laserguns, plasmaguns, railguns, or at least semi-automatics, instead of something that wouldn't have looked out of place in the hands of billy the kid? your guess is as good as mine.

oh, and there's a few example of terrible translation throughout the game too - starting with the achievements. the one that really made me roll my eyes was when i learned that you need a piece of flint in order to start a fire camp. yes, a fire camp, which is presumably a place where fire-parents send their fire-kids for the summer to keep them out of their fire-hair. lovely. i don't really mind those little slips so much, though... they actually kind of add to the sense of period-appropriate authenticity - 'this guy are sick' style, ya know?

regardless, the final tl;dr is that the story-writing is abominable, and the combat and gameplay, taken alone, is way too generic and cookie-cutter to be worth the price of admission. there are way better retro-rpg's around these days, starting with a slew of hd-remakes and re-releases of actual ps1/2-era jrpg...

this is, if not the weirdest game on steam, then certainly in the running. 

go to indonesia, unravel an ancient mystery, learn silat, and date fish. all in a nostalgic pastel color pallette with soothing music playing in the background.

nusakana is like the gonzo lovechild of harvest moon and legend of the river king, and despite english not being its original language, it is clearly a labor of love. in fact, the production values are so high that i think it would have been a cult classic if it had released back in the days of the snes. as is, it commando-crawls at top speed out of steam's rpg maker ghetto, punching komodo dragons in the face the whole way.

if you're willing to play something a bit different, then there's a ton of content in here. day/night cycle, days of the week, quest boards and faction loyalty, rpg combat, fishing, crafting, language-learning, and dating, and a plotline that runs deeper than i would have expected. somehow, rather than turning into an unharmonious kludge, all these elements work together, producing a play experience that is both relaxing and satisfying.

if you liked harvest moon, i'd say this is a solid $15 game. if you like to explore weird avenues of game design, or just the weirder stuff steam has to offer, i'd impulse-buy this on 50% sale.

if nothing i've said above even remotely appeals, then steer clear. this strangeness is probably not for you.
